introduction-what-is-finops.core: FinOps is the operating model that brings financial accountability to variable cloud spend. Engineering, finance and business collaborate to make speed, cost and quality trade-offs with data.

first_principles.problem: Cloud lets engineers spend money instantly with no procurement step, so costs balloon without anyone being accountable.
truths: Cloud spend is decentralised and variable.
Engineers make the purchasing decisions now.

analogy.title: Buying a house vs. paying an electricity bill
analogy.story: Data centres were house purchases planned for months; cloud is a meter that runs continuously based on daily choices.
analogy.breaks: FinOps isn't about cutting costs. It's about maximising value.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Spend grows slower than the business.

check.q: What are the three FinOps lifecycle phases?

phase-1-inform-visibility.core: Inform creates visibility: accurate allocation (tags, accounts), shared-cost splitting, showback, benchmarking, forecasting and unit metrics, so every team sees what it spends and why.

first_principles.problem: A single-line bill ('Purchases: $47,000') makes optimisation impossible.
truths: You can't manage what you can't see.

analogy.title: An itemised credit card statement
analogy.story: Itemisation reveals exactly which purchases drove the total.
analogy.breaks: Visibility without action is just reporting, which is why the later phases exist.

example.title: Inform phase deliverables
example.outcome: the foundation for every later decision.

check.q: What's the main goal of the Inform phase?
check.a: Accurate, timely visibility and allocation of cloud costs to the teams responsible.

phase-2-optimize-efficiency.core: Optimize acts on the visibility through two levers. Usage optimisation (rightsizing, waste removal, scheduling, architecture) is the engineers' lever; rate optimisation (Savings Plans, RIs, spot, negotiated discounts) is usually the central team's.

first_principles.problem: Teams can see their waste but don't systematically reduce it or buy discounts.
truths: Usage and rates are separate levers.
Engineers control usage; a central team usually manages rates.
Optimise usage before committing to rates.
derivation: **Rate**: commitments for the steady baseline, spot for flexible work.

analogy.title: Reducing a household energy bill
analogy.story: Insulate and switch off lights (usage), then negotiate a better tariff (rate).
analogy.breaks: Committing before rightsizing locks in waste.

example.title: An optimisation sprint
flow: Then buy Savings Plans on new baseline (−25% on remaining)

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No commitments are wasted on oversized fleets.

check.q: Why optimise usage before buying commitments?
check.a: Otherwise you commit to paying for waste you could have eliminated.

phase-3-operate-culture.core: Operate makes FinOps continuous: governance and policies, automation, regular cost reviews, KPIs, training and incentives, so savings stick and cost-aware decisions become habit.

first_principles.problem: A $200k saving quarter is followed by the same waste building up again.
truths: Culture comes from routines and incentives.
derivation: Hold **regular reviews** (weekly anomalies, monthly team reviews).

analogy.title: Fitness: a gym habit vs. a crash diet
analogy.story: A crash diet works briefly; a routine keeps results.
analogy.breaks: Too much governance slows engineers, so automate rather than gatekeep.

example.title: An operating rhythm
example.outcome: FinOps becomes how the organisation works.

check.q: What's the purpose of the Operate phase?
check.a: To embed FinOps continuously through governance, automation, rituals and culture so the gains persist.

the-six-finops-principles.core: The FinOps principles: teams collaborate; everyone takes ownership of their cloud usage; a centralised team drives FinOps; reports should be accessible and timely; decisions are driven by the business value of the cloud; take advantage of the variable cost model.

first_principles.problem: Without guiding principles, FinOps degrades into cost policing or finance-only reporting.
truths: Value, not cost alone, should drive decisions.
derivation: Have a **central enabling team** (rates, tooling, standards).
Make data **accessible and timely**; decide on **business value**; use **variable cost** to your advantage.

analogy.title: Rules of a shared household
analogy.story: Everyone contributes, owns their mess, one person manages the bills, receipts are visible, spend on what matters, and adjust as needs change.
analogy.breaks: Principles need concrete practices behind them, or they stay slogans.

check.q: Does FinOps always mean reducing spend?
check.a: No. Decisions are driven by business value, which can justify spending more.
